title: Greenwashing

definition.text: Advertising or public relations meant to mislead people into believing an organization's products, goals or policies are good for the environment.

facts.text: The word blends 'green' with 'whitewashing'.
Firms greenwash to win legitimacy with environmentally minded people, to look responsible to the wider public, and to distance themselves from their own or their suppliers' environmental failings.
A common rule of thumb: an organization is greenwashing if it spends far more on advertising a green image than on actually acting in environmentally sound ways.
With no agreed definition, consumers and regulators can find it hard to decide whether a given case is greenwashing.
New York environmentalist Jay Westerveld coined the term in a 1986 essay on hotels urging guests to reuse towels to 'save the environment', which mainly cut laundry costs.
A 2020 European Union study found over 50% of examined environmental claims were vague, misleading or unfounded, and 40% were unsubstantiated.
Many companies pledged net-zero emissions after the 2015 Paris Agreement, but critics say they make unfeasible plans instead of actually cutting emissions.
Critics argue that widespread greenwashing, with weak regulation and enforcement, makes consumers doubt all green claims and weakens their power to push firms toward greener practices.

definition.text: A list of seven kinds of misleading environmental claims, set out by the consultancy TerraChoice in 2007 to help shoppers spot them.

facts.text: The sins are hidden trade-off, no proof, vagueness, worshipping false labels, irrelevance, lesser of two evils, and fibbing (a plainly false claim).
A 'hidden trade-off' calls a product green on the basis of a narrow set of attributes while ignoring other important environmental issues.
TerraChoice reported that by 2010 about 95% of U.S. consumer products claiming to be green committed at least one of the sins.
The United Nations lists similar tactics, such as announcing future environmental milestones without real plans to reach them, or highlighting one good practice while doing nothing else.

definition.text: Ways of sorting greenwashing by where the misleading claim or misconduct arises: in a firm itself, in its suppliers, in a product, or across the whole organization.

facts.text: Direct greenwashing is when a firm's own processes contradict its environmental claims; indirect greenwashing is when a supplier's false claims harm the firm it supplies.
Vicarious greenwashing is when a firm that calls itself green partners with a polluting supplier and is blamed for that supplier's misconduct.
At product level, 'claim' greenwashing uses misleading statements or unverified labels such as 'eco-friendly', while 'executional' greenwashing relies on green colours and nature imagery.
Firm-level greenwashing promotes sustainability in campaigns while the company's operations keep damaging the environment.

definition.text: Giving an organization or product a name that falsely suggests it is environmentally friendly.

facts.text: Industrial firms and associations use such front groups to dispute scientific findings that threaten their business, for example denial of human-caused global warming by fossil energy companies.
Deceptive names are used because openly arguing for environmentally damaging activities is hard when environmental protection enjoys broad public support.
ExxonMobil supported more than 100 climate denial organizations and spent about 20 million U.S. dollars on greenscamming groups.

definition.text: Laws, codes and guidelines that govern what businesses may say about the environmental benefits of their products, aimed at curbing greenwashing.

facts.text: Rules on misleading environmental claims differ worldwide, ranging from criminal liability to fines to voluntary guidelines.
The US Federal Trade Commission's voluntary 'green guides' say any qualifications must be clear, prominent and understandable enough to prevent deception.
The UK Competition and Markets Authority published a Green Claims Code in September 2021 to protect consumers from misleading environmental claims.
A January 2021 European Commission review found that green claims on 42 percent of consumer websites examined were likely false and misleading.
In June 2024 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled that firms advertising as 'climate neutral' must define the term, because it is otherwise too vague.
EU rules require companies with over 250 staff and €40 million turnover to disclose ESG information, which is expected to help combat greenwashing.
Firms may also seek environmental certification so that independent checks verify their green claims.

title: Bluewashing

definition.text: False or misleading claims about how an action affects water and ocean environments, by analogy with greenwashing.

facts.text: Bluewashing is named as a term closely akin to greenwashing.
It is used in discussions of the blue economy, the sustainable development of coastal and ocean resources.

notes: No page of its own; passes the two-page mention test (Greenwashing, Blue economy). The Greenwashing sentence that follows uses the term for CSR claims, so senses differ slightly.

definition.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at a time.

facts.text: Uniform planting, care and harvest make monocultures easy and efficient in the short term, often giving higher yields and lower costs.
Over the long term they are more prone to disease and pest outbreaks because of reduced local biodiversity and nutrient depletion.
Diversity can be added over time through crop rotation or in space through polyculture or intercropping.
Monoculture and synthetic fertilizers have reduced the extra land needed to grow food, which is called land sparing.
Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soils and encourage soil-borne disease.
Declining soil health leads to more synthetic fertilizer, whose excess nitrogen can contaminate drinking water and feed algal blooms.
Over 600 million liters of pesticides are sprayed each year after pest outbreaks, harming nearby small farms and community health.
Agroecology, silvopastoral systems and mixed-species plantations are common alternatives that keep productivity while preserving biodiversity.

definition.text: Planting crops, or raising animals, with little or no genetic variation across a whole region.

facts.text: When all plants in a region are genetically alike, one disease they cannot resist can wipe out entire crops.
Ireland's reliance on a single potato variety, the 'lumper', led to the Great Famine of 1845–1849 once Phytophthora infestans arrived.
Gros Michel bananas, all clones, fell to Fusarium wilt, and growers switched to the Cavendish by the early 1960s; it faces similar risk.
Genetic monoculture in the global food supply is a significant threat to food security.

definition.text: Plantations made up of a single tree species, often grown for timber.

facts.text: After deforestation, single-species afforestation has become popular for ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration to fight climate change.
Eucalyptus, pines and acacias are common choices in the tropics and Global South, often imported species that replace native forest.
Such schemes may bring global climate benefit yet cause local harm, including soil depletion and altered water cycles.
Single-species forests reduce biodiversity, lowering forest productivity and native plant and animal populations, and weakening resistance to pests and disease.
Plantations often offer few local jobs, and profits tend to follow a boom-and-bust pattern rarely reinvested in the land.
In China, a shift to low-cost monoculture of mostly red pine meant trees that died never delivered their expected carbon offset.

definition.text: Foreign control over farming driven by large-scale production of agricultural commodities for export, often grown as monocultures.

facts.text: Large tropical monocultures have reduced local and indigenous food sovereignty, food security and access to land and water.
More than 46 million hectares of soy have been planted in South America, while over half a million hectares are deforested each year for cultivation.
Repeated single-crop cultivation exhausts soil nutrients and microbial diversity, increasing reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

definition.text: A tree plantation that grows several species together instead of one.

facts.text: Several studies show well-managed mixed-species plantations earn more from timber than monocultures.
Mixed-species forests store more carbon and hold more biodiversity.
They remain less common because of a mistaken belief that they cost more and are harder to manage.

title: Tree planting

definition.text: Transplanting young tree seedlings into the ground, usually for forestry, land reclamation or landscaping.

facts.text: In forestry it is called reforestation where land was recently forested and afforestation where it was not.
Done properly it can regenerate a deforested area, but a planted forest rarely matches the biodiversity and complexity of a natural one.

Outside interests often profit more from fast-growing species such as eucalyptus or pine, whose plantations bring far smaller biodiversity benefits than native forest and are often controversial as offsets.
Many environmentalists argue that only native trees should be planted, to help native ecosystems regrow.
Planted forests covered an estimated 312 million ha in 2025, 8% of all forest area, and grew by 120 million ha since 1990.
Almost all plantation forests (95%) in South America are of introduced species.
Tree-planting initiatives can harm biodiversity, especially in tropical savannas.

contested_note: Plantation offset projects using fast-growing non-native species are described as frequently controversial.

title: Tree planting for climate mitigation
article: Tree planting#Role in climate change mitigation

definition.text: Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it, as a way to limit climate change.

facts.text: Forests act as carbon sinks and take up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
Forests can switch from sinks to sources: in 2019 they absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Avoiding deforestation beats clearing and replanting, which causes irreversible biodiversity loss and soil damage; new forests also take several decades to deliver comparable carbon benefits.
Scientists call protecting and restoring carbon-rich, long-lived ecosystems, especially natural forests, 'the major climate solution'.
An estimate of room for 0.9 billion ha more tree canopy has been criticized; counting albedo and other feedbacks, the area that truly cools is 20-80% lower.
Such planting would store 205 billion tons of carbon only if the trees survive future climate stress to maturity.
Stored carbon must not return to the air through burning or rotting when trees die.
A meta-analysis found mixed-species plantations would store more carbon than single-species ones.

contested_note: The global estimate of land available for climate-cooling tree planting has been criticized as far too high.

definition.text: The share of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects.

facts.text: It runs from 0, a black body absorbing everything, to 1, a surface reflecting everything.
Fresh snow reflects about 0.9 to 0.95 of visible light, while charcoal reflects about 0.04.
Oceans and most forests have low albedo, while deserts are among the most reflective landforms.
Albedo shapes climate by setting how much radiation a planet absorbs.
Deciduous trees have an albedo of about 0.15 to 0.18 and conifers about 0.09 to 0.15.
Land-use changes such as deforestation, farming and urbanization alter albedo and can perturb Earth's energy balance.

definition.text: The way dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling gained when new trees store carbon.

facts.text: Forests have low albedo because they absorb most ultraviolet and visible light for photosynthesis.
In snowy regions, treeless winter albedo is 10% to 50% higher than nearby forest, because snow does not cover trees as readily.
Hadley Centre studies found new tropical and midlatitude forests tended to cool, while high-latitude forests such as in Siberia were neutral or perhaps warming.
For snowy evergreen forests, the albedo effect can be large enough that clearing them causes net cooling.
A 2023 study of 176 flux stations found afforestation may cause moderate warming for about 20 years before turning to significant cooling.
Tropical reforestation helps form clouds that reflect sunlight, while boreal reforestation swaps bright snow for dark canopy and helps the climate less.
Evapotranspiration from trees is usually treated as net cooling, so the overall effect of deforestation depends heavily on local climate.

definition.text: A self-reinforcing loop in which melting snow or ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more heat and cause more melting.

facts.text: Snow albedo ranges from about 0.9 when fresh to about 0.4 when melting and 0.2 when dirty.
It is one of the main reinforcing climate feedbacks, along with water vapour and the net effect of clouds.
Melting Arctic ice leaves darker water and ground, so less heat is reflected back to space.

title: Human-caused albedo change
article: Albedo#Changes to albedo due to human activities

definition.text: Changes in how much sunlight the land reflects caused by human land use such as cities, farms and deforestation.

facts.text: Urban areas are commonly 0.01–0.02 lower in albedo than nearby cropland, which adds to warming.
Raising urban albedo on purpose can ease the urban heat island effect.
A 2022 estimate found that raising albedo by 0.1 across the world's urban areas would cool as much as absorbing ~44 Gt of CO2.

definition.text: A review that maps the concepts, language and data around a topic, refining its search as it goes, to gauge how much evidence an area holds.

facts.text: It often comes before a systematic review, to judge whether a full review is possible or worthwhile.
Its methods may change during the work, sometimes departing from the original protocol.
A related mapping review or systematic map sorts existing literature by quantity, quality and study design to show where more research is needed.

title: Limitations of systematic reviews
article: Systematic review#Out-dated or risk of bias

definition.text: The ways systematic reviews can mislead, through biased inputs, outdated searches or poor reporting, despite being treated as the strongest evidence.

facts.text: A 2003 review of 300 studies found systematic reviews were not all equally reliable.
Of 100 reviews monitored, 7% needed updating on publication, another 4% within a year and another 11% within 2 years.
Around half of clinical trials never report results, and 'positive' trials were twice as likely to be published as 'negative' ones, skewing what reviews can find.
Many reviews comply poorly with reporting guidelines and have weak, hard-to-reproduce search strategies.

verification.title: Epidemiology and Reporting Characteristics of Systematic Reviews
verification.evidence: Only half (150 [50.0%]) of the reviews used the term "systematic review" or "meta-analysis" in the title or abstract.

verification.title: How Quickly Do Systematic Reviews Go Out of Date? A Survival Analysis
verification.evidence: MEASUREMENTS: Quantitative signals for updating were changes in statistical significance or relative changes in effect magnitude of at least 50% involving 1 of the primary outcomes of the original systematic review or any mortality outcome.
verification.note: 100 reviews, 7% at publication, 15% within 1 yr, 23% within 2 yr match cumulative facts; 50% is effect-size threshold

definition.text: A forest planted to produce large volumes of wood, usually as a single-species monoculture.

facts.text: Managed timber forests commonly yield 1 to 3 cubic meters of wood per hectare per year, while fast-growing plantations commonly yield 20 to 30 or more.
In 2000 plantations made up 5% of global forest but supplied an estimated 35% of the world's roundwood.
Industrial plantations are large, even-aged blocks of one or two species, often bred for fast growth and pest resistance.
Trees are usually harvested after 10 to 60 years, so plantations lack the growth, soil, wildlife and decaying dead wood of old-growth forest.
Fast-wood plantations or fiber farms, started in Brazil in the 1970s, run on rotations as short as 5 to 15 years.
Eucalyptus is the most widely planted plantation tree worldwide.
Long-term carbon storage depends on what happens to the harvested wood.
Fiber plantations offer local people a much narrower range of services than the natural forest they replace, sometimes ignoring local rights.

title: Plantations and natural forest loss

definition.text: The argument over whether high-yield plantations spare natural forests from logging or instead replace them.

facts.text: In principle plantations need less land for the same wood; in New Zealand 19% of the forest area supplies 99% of industrial roundwood.
According to the FAO, about 7% of natural closed forest lost in the tropics is converted to plantations, and 93% to agriculture and other uses.
An estimated 15% of plantations in tropical countries are set up on closed-canopy natural forest.
Using plantations to cut carbon dioxide is challenged because the stored CO2 is eventually released after harvest.

contested_note: Foresters say plantations reduce pressure on natural forest, while in practice some plantations replace it.

title: Introduced species in plantations

definition.text: Planting tree species far outside their natural range because they grow fast and suit industrial use.

facts.text: Globally, 44 percent of plantation forests are made up mainly of introduced species.
Introduced species dominate planted forests in South America (88%), Oceania (75%) and East and Southern Africa (65%), but are only 1%, 3% and 8% in North America, West and Central Asia, and Europe.
Pine, spruce and eucalyptus are the classic examples, valued for fast growth and tolerance of degraded farmland.

notes: Shares differ by base: Tree planting S:ecd77a89b1f6 gives 95% introduced for South American plantation forests; Tree plantation S:d167d131e0a8 gives 88% for South American planted forests (planted forest is a wider category). Not treated as a conflict.
